_about: How every character sounds and how each line is acted, for tools/voices-gemini.mjs. 'voices' designs one custom Gemini voice per character (age, accent, timbre live here, never in a style). 'context' is the default delivery for each kind of line. 'lines' overrides single lines: the key is the start of the spoken words; 'style' is the acting direction, 'say' (optional) is the same words with Gemini vocal tags like <sigh>, <chuckle> or <short pause>. Change anything here and run npm run voices:gemini again: only the lines you changed are re-rendered.

cole.design: Agent Danny Cole, an American man of about 24 in 1933. A light, quick, bright young voice with a slightly nervous edge; earnest and eager to please; speeds up when he gets excited. Plain Midwestern accent.

hart.design: Inspector Rowan Hart, an American air-mail inspector in his late forties, 1933. A low, slightly gravelly, unhurried voice; dry, understated and weary, like a hard-boiled narrator who has seen too much.

pryce.design: Cornelius Pryce, a 62-year-old American airline tycoon in 1933. A rich, theatrical baritone; charming and imperious, a man used to an audience.

vivienne.design: Vivienne Pryce, a 38-year-old former stage actress in 1933. A warm, smoky contralto with a polished mid-Atlantic stage accent; amused and theatrical, every line slightly performed.

billie.design: Captain Billie Strand, a 34-year-old American woman pilot in 1933. Fast, rough, cheerful and brash, with a slightly husky voice that breaks into laughter easily; plain-spoken.

lindqvist.design: Doctor Matthias Lindqvist, a 56-year-old Swedish physician living in America. A soft, gentle tenor with a light Swedish accent; measured and anxious, speaks in careful full sentences, with a slight hesitation before difficult words.

julian.design: Julian Ferreira-Blake, a 41-year-old airline executive in 1933. Silky, unhurried and impeccably polite, with a refined transatlantic accent; warm on the surface, cold underneath.

ox.design: Abel 'Ox' Brennan, a huge, gentle 33-year-old American mechanic. A very deep, slow, soft voice with long pauses; plain rural American; he never raises his voice.

tamsin.design: Tamsin Quill, a 29-year-old American secretary in 1933. A dry, clipped, deadpan alto with a smoker's rasp; sarcastic and quick.

hobbs.design: Walter Hobbs, a 67-year-old American radio operator. An old, cheerful, rambling voice, a little too loud because he is half-deaf; warm rural accent with a pipe-smoker's crackle.

clementine.design: Clementine Pryce, a 21-year-old American woman who has hidden underground for two years. A quiet, soft voice, hoarse from disuse; careful, formal, old-fashioned phrasing; quiet intensity.

context.cole.radio: speaking into a crackling radio over wind, voice slightly raised
context.cole.briefing: clear and earnest, briefing his boss
context.cole.people: conversational, sizing people up, a little gossipy
context.cole.reaction: struck by a discovery, excited, speeding up
context.hart.telegram: reading a telegram aloud, terse and flat, a short pause at each full stop
context.intro.coleSky: frightened, shouting over a roaring engine
context.intro.hartSky: dry and calm, deadpan, raised over engine noise
context.intro.hobbs: friendly, raised voice over the wind
context.intro.pryce: a grand theatrical toast, the last words dropping to a hush
context.clem.dark: calm and quiet, a voice from the dark some distance away
context.clem.question: quiet, testing
context.clem.confession: hushed and steady, holding back tears
context.cylinder: panicked, shouting over a screaming engine, terrified

I hear you, Chief. Mostly..style: speaking into a crackling radio, raised voice, a bit frazzled

If it were my case.say: If it were my case, which, <chuckle> thank God, it isn't...

We're down. We're actually down..say: We're down. We're actually down. <laugh> I'm never complaining about trains again.

The last postcard you get from her.style: warm and moved, a hush on the last word

In my room with a book I wasn't reading..style: languid, then haunted at the end

So someone else wound it..style: the mask slipping, realizing, a little frightened

Poison. How very theatrical..style: dark amusement, then a hint of grief

Inspector. If you're here to tell me not.style: wry and brash, a laugh in her voice
Inspector. If you're here to tell me not.say: Inspector. If you're here to tell me not to touch anything, I already broke the door down. <short pause> With an axe. <laugh>

He didn't answer at six..style: blunt, fast, a little shaken underneath

A cockpit fire in '29..style: curt, guarded, shutting the subject down

...Fine. Yes..style: giving in, frustrated, then fast and defiant

That's evidence, is it?.say: <snort> That's evidence, is it? Looks like junk to me.

Inspector. A terrible business..style: nervous, insisting a little too much

Heart failure. Almost certainly..style: nervous, insisting, faltering at the end

Digitalis. Foxglove..style: careful and precise, defensive at the end

Cyanide. Yes. I smelled it..style: broken, ashamed, close to tears, halting
Cyanide. Yes. I smelled it..say: <sigh> Cyanide. Yes. I smelled it. God forgive me, I smelled it and I said heart failure because I was afraid of what an inquest would find. Not who killed him. <short pause> What else.

That she was leaving him.style: cool, precise, a quiet warning at the end

Business is business, Inspector..style: the smooth mask slipping, cold and clipped

I said that's all..style: embarrassed and angry, flustered, a little louder than he means

Old fuel line..say: Old fuel line. <short pause> Under everything. I'm not supposed to talk about it.

I did what I was told..style: anguished, voice cracking, breaking off unfinished

She needs things..style: slow, quiet, protective, after a long silence

It's only a lamp..say: It's only a lamp. She reads by it. Don't take that away. <short pause> I mean. Nobody reads down there.

He told me to clear his diary.style: flat and dry, a beat of unease at the end

Nineteen, three, seventeen..style: deadpan, dark humour on the last word

Yes. Five hundred a month.style: a humourless laugh, then flat and cold
Yes. Five hundred a month.say: <chuckle> Yes. Five hundred a month for the real weather report. Blackmail isn't murder, Inspector. Dead men don't pay.

The old fuel culvert.style: rambling, then spooked on the last words

Every one, Inspector..style: earnest, a little hurt, firm at the end

Under the office? Well I never..style: astonished, then spooked, talking himself out of it

Eh? Speak up, Inspector..say: Eh? <short pause> Speak up, Inspector. Oh, that. Can't say I know.

You don't know. Not really..style: quiet, wry, a small breathless laugh at the wrong moment
You don't know. Not really..say: You don't know. Not really. Come back when you do, Inspector. I'm not going anywhere. <chuckle> That was rather the point.

The man upstairs stumbles on his Q..style: oddly polite, a small laugh at the wrong moment
The man upstairs stumbles on his Q..say: The man upstairs stumbles on his Q. I copied him. <chuckle> It seemed polite.

I put it in the decanter that afternoon.style: hushed, remembering, voice thinning at the end

He knew the mount was cracked..style: quiet anger, trembling, bitter at the end

You brought a boy with you..style: soft, tender, a small sad smile

I died, Inspector..style: quiet, a hint of dark amusement
